body.hook: Every time your phone buzzes, you probably reach for it before thinking. You weren't born doing that. You learned it, through the same process a Russian scientist discovered while studying dogs that drooled at the sound of footsteps.

study.title: Pavlov's Discovery
study.question: How do we learn to connect events?
study.passage:
Ivan Pavlov (1890s–1900s) was studying digestion in dogs when he noticed they drooled before food arrived, at the sound of the assistant's footsteps. He tested it:
• Before learning: food (UCS) → drooling (UCR); bell (neutral) → no drooling.
• During learning: bell + food, many times.
• After learning: bell (CS) → drooling (CR).
Extinction: If the bell rings again and again with no food, drooling fades. Spontaneous recovery: After a rest, the bell may trigger drooling again briefly. Generalization: A similar sound triggers drooling. Discrimination: The dog learns to respond only to the exact bell.
Watson and "Little Albert" (1920): John B. Watson conditioned a baby to fear a white rat by pairing it with a loud noise; the fear generalized to other furry things. The study is now considered deeply unethical: no consent from informed parents in the modern sense, distress to a child and no deconditioning.
Everyday examples: phone notification sounds, the smell of a hospital, a song that reminds you of someone, ads pairing products with happy music.

examples.problem: A child gets a shot (pain, fear) at a clinic that smells of disinfectant. Later the smell causes fear. Label it.
examples.answer: UCS shot; UCR fear; CS smell; CR fear of the smell

practice.q: How did Watson condition Little Albert?
practice.a: Paired a white rat with a loud noise.

practice.q: Why is the UCR and CR often the same behaviour?
practice.a: The same response is triggered first naturally, then by the learned stimulus.

practice.q: Why was the Little Albert study unethical?
practice.a: It caused distress to a child without proper consent or deconditioning.

practice.q: How might exposure therapy use extinction?
practice.a: Repeated exposure to a feared stimulus without harm weakens the fear.

practice.q: How do advertisers use classical conditioning?
practice.a: They pair products with pleasant images or music.

practice.q: Explain your phone-buzz reaction using conditioning.
practice.a: The buzz (CS) was paired with messages (UCS), so it triggers checking and anticipation (CR).
